```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(rmai)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = mai_available())
```

[mai](https://github.com/mai-lib/mai) is the compiled statistical computing
language from Brendan McArdle's 2018 University of Auckland PhD thesis. It
reads like R, but compiles loops and function calls to fast bytecode. rmai
lets you use it from R.

## Getting the executable

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rmai::mai_install()          # downloads mai-lib/mai and builds it (Linux)
rmai::mai_install("~/src/mai", portable = TRUE)   # or from a local checkout
```

`mai_path()` shows which executable rmai will use. You can also point it at
one with `options(rmai.path = "/path/to/mai")` or the `MAI_PATH` environment
variable.

```{r}
mai_available()
```

## Running code

```{r}
mai_run("print(sum(1:100))")

mai_run(c(
  "const harmonic = function(int n) : double {",
  "    var s = 0.0",
  "    for(int i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 1) s = s + 1.0 / i",
  "    s",
  "}",
  "print(harmonic(1000000))"
))
```

Errors in mai code become R warnings by default (`error = "stop"` makes them
R errors):

```{r}
out <- mai_run('stop("something went wrong")')
attr(out, "error")
```

`mai_source("script.mai")` runs a file, with `include` paths resolved
relative to the file's directory.

## Passing R data in and getting R values back

`mai_eval()` is the most natural way to use mai from R. Named arguments
become `const` globals in mai, the expression is evaluated there, and the
result comes back as an R vector or array. Data moves in binary, so doubles
are exact and large inputs are cheap.

```{r}
x <- runif(1e5)
mai_eval("sum(sqrt(x))", x = x)
sum(sqrt(x))
```

The expression can be a whole block. Here a loop that would be slow in
plain R runs as compiled mai, with a helper defined in `.setup`:

```{r}
mai_eval(
  "var n = length(x), s = 0.0
   for(int i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 1) s = s + sq(x[i] - 0.5)
   s / n",
  x = x,
  .setup = "const sq = function(double v) : double v * v"
)
```

Integer and logical vectors keep their types, matrices keep their shape,
and `NA` survives the trip:

```{r}
m <- matrix(c(1, NA, 3, 4), 2)
mai_eval("m * 10.0", m = m)
mai_eval("!b", b = c(TRUE, NA, FALSE))
```

## mai chunks in R Markdown and Quarto

Loading rmai registers a `mai` knitr engine. Each chunk runs in a fresh mai
process. To build on an earlier chunk, label it and name it in
`mai.include`:

````
```{mai, helpers}`r ''`
const dotprod = function(x, y) sum(x * y)
const norm = function(x) sqrt(dotprod(x, x))
```
````

```{mai, helpers}
const dotprod = function(x, y) sum(x * y)
const norm = function(x) sqrt(dotprod(x, x))
```

````
```{mai, mai.include = "helpers"}`r ''`
print(norm(vec(3.0, 4.0)))
```
````

```{mai, mai.include = "helpers"}
print(norm(vec(3.0, 4.0)))
```

## Comparing with R

`mai_compare()` times a `run()` function defined in each language:

```{r}
mai_compare(
  "const fib = function(n) if(n <= 2) 1 else fib(n - 2) + fib(n - 1)
   const run = function() fib(24)",
  "fib <- function(n) if (n <= 2) 1 else fib(n - 2) + fib(n - 1)
   run <- function() fib(24)",
  reps = 3
)
```

See the [mai documentation](https://github.com/mai-lib/mai/tree/main/docs),
especially "Differences from R", before writing much mai: for example `7 / 2`
is `3`, and assigning to an undeclared variable inside a function sets a
global.
